claims.text: Multi-element chemical complexity enhances lattice distortion in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion increases dislocation pinning in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion alters phonon behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Increased dislocation pinning and altered phonon behavior jointly explain the high-temperature mechanical strength and thermoelastic response of refractory high-entropy alloys.
Substituting refractory elements with elements having more similar atomic radii will reduce lattice distortion while preserving the alloy's refractory character.
The degree of lattice distortion mediates dislocation mobility.
The degree of lattice distortion modifies phonon dispersion.
Lattice distortion hinders dislocation motion and thereby enhances yield strength.
Lattice distortion affects vibrational modes and consequently modifies elastic moduli.
Lattice distortion affects vibrational modes and consequently modifies thermal-expansion behavior.
Reducing lattice distortion will diminish dislocation-pinning and vibrational-mode effects, producing more conventional mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
At 1000–1200 °C, alloys with higher lattice distortion should exhibit significantly higher yield strength than reduced-distortion control alloys tested under the same conditions.
At 1000–1200 °C, alloys with higher lattice distortion should exhibit a different temperature dependence of elastic modulus than reduced-distortion controls.
At 1000–1200 °C, alloys with higher lattice distortion should exhibit a different thermal-expansion coefficient or response than reduced-distortion controls.
The proposed mechanism applies only when the compared alloys are chemically homogeneous and lack significant microsegregation or secondary-phase formation.
Grain size, residual stress, and microstructural evolution during high-temperature exposure may also contribute to the measured mechanical and thermoelastic responses.
